title: Don't detect PlainActionFuture deadlock on concurrent complete

timeline.message:
Don't detect PlainActionFuture deadlock on concurrent complete

Closes #110360
timeline.author: Nick Tindall

timeline.body:
Closes #110360
Closes #110181 

I don't love the test for this, but it does reproduce the issue reliably. Any suggestions for making it less verbose are appreciated.
I imagine we stay in this state extremely briefly (and rarely) as we're just waiting on two assignments and the release, perhaps busy wait is OK here?

reply.body: We could also use some other synchronisation mechanism here to wait/notify (that didn't add the waiter to the waiters for the `Sync`), but that might be overkill?
Seems ok to me; possibly this is even more efficient, not that efficiency particularly matters in these cases.
Seems fine to me as well. I think `acquire` internally also does busy waiting.

timeline.body: The issue only manifests in the moment the `PlainActionFuture` is first resolved, this test reproduces fairly quickly when we do the above. I wish we didn't have to create objects in a tight loop.

timeline.author: Nick Tindall

timeline.body: This test will unfortunately run the full 250ms in the happy case, on my desktop it seemed to fail around the 80ms mark fairly consistently before the fix.

reply.body: I'd rather a test which fails _sometimes_ but always runs quickly, because we run this so often in CI that it'll catch the bug pretty soon anyway.
Cool, I reduced to 20ms which is still surprisingly reliable.

That doesn't seem to trigger it on my machine (It's been running for >5000 times without a failure so far). I will try and inline the logic so we don't need the inner class. I'm sure it can be made simpler.
Weird, it fails pretty reliably for me. Although 5k iterations isn't very many.
Try running with `-Dtests.iters=1000 -Dtests.failfast=true`, no need to wait for seconds+ for Gradle to start up on each iteration.

I'm not sure what the difference is, but I can't get it to fail. This M3 MacBook seems to eat race conditions for breakfast (I also had trouble reproducing [this one](https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/109866)).

I ran for 800,000 iterations which took ~48 minutes and produced zero failures, where the latest iteration of my longer test fails almost immediately. While I accept that CI Is probably going to yield these failures more reliably, I think it's probably best if we have a test that reproduces on typical dev hardware.

Some theories on why the longer test is more reliable
- it produces ~20 `PlainActionFuture`s, so there's 20x the opportunity for it to occur (it can only occur once per future)
- the threads hitting `onResponse` are hot, possibly running JIT-ed code, as opposed to just woken up from a wait. Perhaps this increases the likelihood of the critical piece of concurrency.

> I think it's probably best if we have a test that reproduces on typical dev hardware.

Hmm I think this is the wrong way round - if "typical dev hardware" isn't able to reproduce genuine race conditions that happen in CI/production then I don't think we should work around that by making one specific test more complex. I'd recommend using a GCP machine for long-running repro attempts rather than your laptop since it'll be closer to real production infra.

I think my version of the test is about as slender as it can be now (thanks for the feedback), but I'm OK with replacing it with the much shorter test if you'd prefer.
I'm satisfied that the issue was there and that the change fixes it, and it sounds like that test will fail in CI if we regress, so I'm happy to go with consensus on the cost/benefit of the additional complexity.

timeline.author: Nick Tindall

timeline.body: I think we should try and simplify the test

timeline.author: Nick Tindall
Nick Tindall

timeline.body: No real need to wait on these futures, uncaught exceptions will fail the test anyway and shutting down the threadpool will `join()` all the threads.
Maybe just loop 20 times rather than hammering on `System.currentTimeMillis()`?
Why not use all the threads available? More than 4 normally, but even if the pool is smaller than 4 sometimes it's still a valid test.

reply.body: It blows the test time out to 300ms+ on my machine because of the additional synchronisation. 4 threads takes < 100ms but still reliably reproduces the issue.
Ok let's use `Math.min(threadPool.info(executorName).getMax(), 4)` rather than failing the test if the threadpool is smaller than 4, and add a comment about why.

timeline.author: Nick Tindall

timeline.body: We can just use `execute()` now that we don't care about the result - no need to wrap the task in a `RunnableFuture`.
Would it help to wait on the future to be completed too?

reply.body: I actually don't think so, I tried replacing the sleep with a wait and that made the test unreliable. I measured, and on my machine each thread completed that loop about 800,000 times in the ~20ms so I feel waiting on the future (in addition to the sleep) is at best redundant and at worst interfering with the behaviour under test.

timeline.body: Could you expand this comment to describe why we're creating multiple futures, recording the investigations you've done in this area?
Is this assumption necessary any more?

reply.body:
Yes, because
```java
    @Override
    public void onFailure(Exception e) {
        assert assertCompleteAllowed();  // <----- only tested when assertions enabled
        ...
```
Sure, but the test is still valid either way AFAICT. I mean most tests make stronger checks if assertions are enabled, but that doesn't mean we should suppress them all like this.

timeline.body: Ok I think the test is simple enough now for my tastes, although IMO it deserves a few more comments explaining why it's not any simpler.
